summary:
NEBULA: AI-Assisted Mental Well-Being Monitor for Deep-Space Crews
Developed by Team Astro 911
NEBULA is a hardware and software prototype that supports the mental well-being of astronauts on deep-space missions. Built on an Arduino UNO Q with an LCD screen and USB hub, and programmed in Python, HTML and CSS, it monitors each crew member's mental state and offers personalized support to help them stay well. NEBULA can play music, guide breathing exercises and suggest light, engaging activities. Crew members can also ask it questions, such as how to sleep better or how to shift their focus away from difficult thoughts.
Deep-space missions mean months away from home, isolation, unusual daylight cycles, radiation and constant noise, all of which take a real toll on mental health. NEBULA gives crews a simple, calming way to relax and stay mentally resilient. It is designed to support, not overwhelm. Wherever possible, it uses existing NASA data through APIs and fits within NASA's current health frameworks.
As a prototype, NEBULA will need further development with mental health and space medicine experts to fine-tune its guidance for real missions.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works
NEBULA is an AI-assisted mental well-being companion for astronauts on long deep-space missions such as a journey to Mars. It runs on an Arduino UNO Q connected to an LCD screen. Crew members answer short multiple-choice check-ins about mood, stress and sleep, with no typing required. NEBULA combines these answers with health data from existing NASA datasets through APIs, including heart rate, blood pressure, sleep patterns and pre-flight medical records. It then produces a real-time well-being report.

Based on the results, NEBULA offers personalized support. It can play calming music, guide breathing exercises and suggest light, engaging activities. Crew members can also ask questions, such as how to sleep better or how to shift away from difficult thoughts, and an on-board language model (Qwen 3.5) answers. If NEBULA detects a serious concern, a red light alerts the crew and guided first-aid steps begin. Reports can be shared with doctors on Earth for a second opinion.

Benefits and intended impact
On a Mars mission, messages to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so real-time psychological support is not possible. NEBULA gives crews immediate support on board while keeping human experts in the loop. Our goal is to help crews stay mentally resilient and to catch problems early, before they affect health, safety or the mission. Future improvements include connect emotionally with the crew and also get details from other data sources through API.

Tools and technologies

  • Hardware: Arduino UNO Q, LCD screen, USB hub, red LED alert
  • Software: Python for logic, AI and API integration; HTML and CSS for the user interface
  • AI: Qwen 3.5 language model for conversational support
  • Data: NASA datasets accessed through APIs

What makes it creative
NEBULA treats mental health as something to support every day, not only during a crisis. It brings together what a crew member says and what their body shows in one view. It also pairs instant AI support on board with a human second opinion from Earth, designed specifically around the long communication delays of deep space.

Factors we considered

  • Privacy: mental health data is highly sensitive, so NEBULA keeps no local database. Data is sent through secure APIs to NASA storage.
  • Simplicity: the interface is calm and quick to use, so it supports the crew without adding to their workload.
  • Fit with NASA systems: NEBULA uses existing NASA data and frameworks wherever possible.
  • Space conditions: microgravity, radiation, isolation and changing daylight cycles may affect both crew health and our results. Testing in analog missions and working with mental health and space medicine experts will be essential next steps.

Future improvements

  • Stronger emotional connection: work with subject matter experts in psychology, psychiatry, space medicine and astronaut support to make NEBULA's conversations, suggestions and activities feel more personal, empathetic and comforting.
  • Better fit with NASA's frameworks: align NEBULA more closely with NASA's existing behavioural health processes, so it complements the work of flight surgeons and psychologists rather than running alongside it.
  • Better use of existing data: draw more deeply on NASA's health and mission datasets to build personal baselines for each crew member, which will improve the accuracy and timing of NEBULA's support.
  • Understanding space conditions: study how microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, changing daylight cycles and constant noise affect both crew well-being and NEBULA's hardware and results. We will then adjust the system to account for them, starting with testing in NASA analog missions
